---
title: "Heat and sleep, explained"
subtitle: "What our research has found, in plain language — and what it does not show"
---

::: {.lead-in}
Singapore's bedrooms are warm. Warm enough, it turns out, to measurably shorten
and fragment the sleep of the people in them.
:::

This page is written for people who are not environmental physiologists —
journalists, policymakers, and anyone who read a headline about our work and
wanted the actual finding. If you want the technical version, the
[research page](research.qmd) has the methods and the
[publications page](publications.qmd) has the papers.

::: {.note-box}
**A caution before the numbers.** Some of the findings below come from analyses
that have not yet completed peer review. They have been presented at scientific
conferences and reported in the press, but they are provisional, and the final
published figures may differ. Where that is true, it is said so explicitly.
Please do not treat any number here as a final published result unless it links
to a paper.
:::

## What we actually measured

Most research on heat and health uses outdoor weather station data. That is
convenient, and it is not where people sleep.

**Project HEATS** measured the inside instead. Across three field waves between
June 2025 and July 2026, we placed environmental sensors in people's bedrooms —
recording temperature, humidity, carbon dioxide and airborne particulates
through the night — while the people sleeping in those rooms wore devices that
recorded how long and how well they slept.

The result is a dataset of **122 participants and 10,303 nights of paired
measurement**: for each night, what the room was doing and what the sleeper was
doing.

A second strand of the work did the same thing in **non-air-conditioned,
multi-occupancy dormitories** housing outdoor workers — rooms with far less
scope to adjust the temperature, and occupants doing physically demanding work
in the heat all day.

## What we found

**Bedrooms in Singapore are hotter than sleep guidance assumes.** The average
nighttime bedroom in our sample sat at around **28°C** — a figure reported in
*The Straits Times* in June 2026. Most international sleep guidance recommends
something closer to 18–21°C. That guidance was developed in temperate climates
and has never been meaningfully tested for the tropics.

**In dormitories, roughly each 1°C warmer meant about 10 minutes less sleep.**
Reported in *Lianhe Zaobao* in June 2026. Ten minutes sounds small. It is not,
when it happens every night, to people whose work the following day is physical
and outdoors, and when the difference between a cool night and a warm one is
several degrees rather than one.

**Heat and behaviour are tangled together, and they have to be separated.** When
a night is hot, people do things: open a window, turn on a fan, move to another
room, go to bed later. So a simple correlation between temperature and sleep
mixes up two different things — what heat does to a sleeping body, and what
people do in response to heat. A large part of our statistical work exists to
pull those apart, because they have completely different policy implications.
Better sleep guidance helps with the first. Affordable cooling helps with the
second.

**The relationship is not a straight line.** Sleep does not degrade smoothly as
the room warms. There appear to be points at which things get worse faster —
which is exactly what a public health agency needs to know, because a threshold
is something you can build an advisory around and a gentle slope is not. Finding
where those points sit, and whether they differ between groups of people, is
the current focus of the analysis.

## What this does *not* show

Being clear about the limits is not modesty; it is what makes the findings
usable.

- **It is not a causal claim about health outcomes.** We measured sleep, not
  cardiovascular disease, not mortality, not workplace injury. The links between
  chronically shortened sleep and those outcomes are established elsewhere in the
  literature — but our data do not themselves demonstrate them.
- **It is not a recommendation to air-condition everything.** Cooling has an
  energy and emissions cost, and one strand of the work specifically tests
  low-energy alternatives. "Turn the air conditioning up" is not the conclusion.
- **It is not a single number that applies to everyone.** Children,
  heat-unacclimatised adults and older adults respond differently to the same
  conditions. A separate programme measures those differences directly, and the
  reason it exists is that a one-size threshold protects the average person and
  nobody else.
- **These are Singapore findings.** They will generalise to some tropical urban
  settings and not to others. Treating them as global is the mistake.

## Why it matters

Singapore is warming, and warm nights are increasing faster than hot days in
many parts of the world. Nighttime is when the body would normally recover from
daytime heat; when it does not get that chance, the strain accumulates.

The practical question is what a heat-health advisory should say, when it should
trigger, and who it should be aimed at. That is why a large part of my work is
evidence synthesis — a review of **113 studies** on how heat-health advisories
are designed and whether they change anything, and a review of **177 records** on
nighttime heat thresholds specifically. Advisories are only as good as the
evidence underneath them, and until recently, nobody had assembled it.

**Name and title.** Dr Michèle Renard — note the grave accent on the first "e"

University of Singapore. On second reference, Dr Renard.

**One line.** Dr Michèle Renard is an environmental physiologist at the National
University of Singapore who studies how heat affects sleep and health.

**Three lines.** Dr Michèle Renard is a Research Fellow at the Yong Loo Lin
School of Medicine, National University of Singapore, leading the statistical
analysis for two national research programmes on heat, sleep and population
health. The work combines large-scale measurement inside people's homes and
dormitories with the evidence synthesis that underpins national heat-health
advice. Dr Renard holds a PhD in Sport, Health and Exercise Sciences and
publishes across environmental physiology and nutritional science.

**Topics I can speak to.** Indoor heat and sleep in tropical climates ·
nighttime temperature thresholds · heat-health warning systems and whether they
work · heat and outdoor workers · statistical methods for environmental health
research.

**Topics I will decline.** Individual medical advice; the health effects of
specific commercial products; anything outside heat, sleep, physiology and
research methods.
